info.summary: One backend for the FoodZone website and mobile app.
info.description:
Every response uses one of two envelopes, so a client never has to branch on
content type:

```json
{ "success": true,  "data": {}, "meta": {} }
{ "success": false, "error": { "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "message": "…", "details": {} } }
```

Clients must branch on `error.code`, never on `error.message`. Codes are a
public contract and are only ever added, never repurposed; messages are reworded
freely.

**Authentication** is either `Authorization: Bearer <access token>` (mobile) or
the `fz_access` httpOnly cookie (web). Both resolve to the same principal.
Access tokens are short-lived; `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` rotates them.

**Authorisation** is per route, stated by the route itself, and composed in a
fixed order: rate limit → authenticate → resolve branch → authorise → validate →
run. Authorisation deliberately runs before validation, so an unauthorised
caller cannot map a payload's shape through validation errors.

**Branch scoping.** Most staff endpoints act at one branch. Where the branch
comes from is listed on each operation, and access to it is checked before the
handler runs.

**Pagination** is cursor-based. A list returns `meta.nextCursor`; pass it back as
`cursor` to fetch the next page. `meta.nextCursor` is `null` on the last page.

**Rate limiting.** Responses carry `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and
`RateLimit-Reset`; a 429 additionally carries `Retry-After`.

**Tracing.** Every response carries `x-request-id`. Quote it when reporting a
fault — a 500 returns the same id in `error.details.requestId`.

**Money** is serialised as a decimal string, never a float, to avoid the
representation errors floats introduce in currency arithmetic.

> **On response bodies:** success payloads are generated as free-form objects.
> The shape of a response comes from Prisma `select` clauses inside the service
> layer, and there is no schema object to read back, so publishing a guessed
> shape would be worse than publishing none. Request bodies, query strings and
> path parameters are all exact — they are generated from the same zod schemas
> the server validates with.

Closes a period. Nothing posts into it afterwards.

Refused while a draft entry still sits in it, and refused while an earlier
period is still open — a closed month with an open one behind it is a set of
figures that can still change underneath a report already published.

Registers a terminal and returns its API key **once**.

The key is stored hashed and is never readable again. A device credential can
post attendance for every employee at that branch, so a key readable from an
admin screen is one that ends up in somebody's notes.

get.description:
Which terminal stopped, and how long ago.

Health is derived from silence rather than reported, because a box that has
fallen off the network cannot tell us it has — and a device quiet for three
days has been losing punches for three days, which nobody finds out about
until payroll.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `attendance_devices.read`. Branch-scoped: the branch is taken from the query parameter `branchId`, and access to it is checked before the handler runs.

post.description:
Links orphaned punches to an employee and enrols the id.

The punches were always real; this is what makes them count. They are marked
unprocessed again so the days they land on get re-derived.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `employees.update`. Rate limit: 60 requests per 1m (`write` class).

A punch typed by a supervisor.

The correction path: derivation treats it like any other punch, but it is
marked MANUAL and carries who added it — vouching for somebody's hours should
have a name against it.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `attendance_punches.create_manual`. Rate limit: 60 requests per 1m (`write` class).

get.summary: List punches that matched no shift
get.description:
Punches for a biometric id nobody is enrolled to.

The queue HR has to work: every row is somebody whose attendance is being
recorded and not counted. Kept rather than dropped, because discarding them
loses real attendance nobody can recover.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `attendance_punches.read`. Branch-scoped: the branch is taken from the query parameter `branchId`, and access to it is checked before the handler runs.

post.description:
Drops the override so the machine's answer applies again.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `attendance.edit`. Rate limit: 60 requests per 1m (`write` class).

Signs off attendance for payroll.

Payroll pays what was approved, not what the terminal recorded — which is the
point of having somebody look at a `MISSING_PUNCH` before an employee loses a
day's pay to a flat battery. Approving those is allowed and reported, because
sometimes the right answer really is "they were here, the device broke".

An approval is a signature, so it is confined to the branches the signer
holds the key at, whether or not the request names one.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `attendance.approve`. Branch-scoped: the branch is taken from the body field `branchId`, and access to it is checked before the handler runs. Rate limit: 60 requests per 1m (`write` class).

Folds punches into days.

Idempotent: the same punches produce the same day, so this is safe nightly,
on demand, and again after a re-sync. Days a supervisor has corrected are
skipped unless `force` is set — a correction that evaporates on the next run
is worse than none at all.

Scoped to the caller's own branches even when they name none, because this

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `attendance.edit`. Branch-scoped: the branch is taken from the body field `branchId`, and access to it is checked before the handler runs. Rate limit: 60 requests per 1m (`write` class).

get.summary: Export part of the catalog as CSV
get.description:
Downloads part of the catalog as CSV.

Returns the file itself rather than the JSON envelope, because the caller is
a browser following a link or a person saving a spreadsheet. What comes out
is exactly what the importer reads back, so export → edit → import is a
round trip.

Rate-limited as a read but on the stricter side: each call is a full table
scan of the catalog.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `catalog.export`. Rate limit: 20 requests per 1m. Audited as `catalog.export`.

200.description: Raw response — see the endpoint notes; not the JSON envelope.

get.description:
The columns each importable resource accepts.

Served rather than only documented so the admin UI can render the column list
and the rules beside the file picker — the moment someone actually needs
them — and so it cannot drift from what the importer enforces.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires any of the permissions `catalog.import`, `catalog.export`.

post.summary: Import catalog records from a CSV
post.description:
Bulk-creates and updates catalog records from a CSV.

Every row is validated before anything is written, and the writes happen in
one transaction: a half-imported catalog, with new prices on some products
and old prices on others, is worse than an import that failed outright.

Send `dryRun: true` first. The response is identical apart from `applied`, so
the same screen can show what would happen and then what did.

A separate permission from editing one product, because this rewrites prices
across the estate in a single call.

Requires an authenticated caller. Requires the permission `catalog.import`. Rate limit: 10 requests per 1m. Audited as `catalog.import`.

is a guardrail enforced in code — a mistyped key in a blob would silently
disable one rather than failing.

with a phone camera, standing at a table.

`/m/{code}` is the printed URL; the web page and the app both call this

genuinely has to write — the camera opens a URL and nothing else ever happens

post.description:
First-run setup: creates the owner account and the first branch.

The only unauthenticated endpoint in the system that creates an account with
administrative rights, so read `bootstrap.service.js` before changing
anything here — the guards are the whole of its security.

**404, not 403, once setup is done.** A system that answers "forbidden" has
told an anonymous caller that a setup endpoint exists and that it is already
claimed. Not found says nothing, and is also true: there is no setup to
perform.

One deliberate asymmetry: body validation runs before these guards, so a
malformed payload answers 400 whether or not the system is set up. That
reveals only that this software is running, which any deployment of it
shows anyway. What it must not reveal is whether the installation is
*unclaimed*, and it does not: a well-formed request without the right token
answers 404 in both states, identically.

The token travels in a header, not the body: it stays out of the validated
payload, out of anything that logs a request body, and out of the schema
that describes what an installation is. It is compared in constant time.

Public — no authentication required. Rate limit: 20 requests per 15m (`auth` class).
